notes: Independently found the same fastify-type-provider-zod blocker and went deeper: full peerDependency compatibility matrix across its 4.0.2/5.x/6.x/7.0.0 releases.
More thorough than with_skill on the single most important finding in this eval, while still cheaper/faster than with_skill's own eval-1 and eval-2 runs.

The only expectation that discriminated between configurations across all 3 evals was 'has_per_dependency_size_table' in eval 1 - baseline gave top-5 bullet lists instead of a full per-dependency table. Every other expectation passed in both configurations on every eval.

Baseline (no skill) independently found the same high-value findings as with_skill in 2 of 3 evals (mcp's pnpm/npm layout mismatch in eval 2; the fastify-type-provider-zod peer-dependency blocker in eval 3) - and was arguably more thorough than with_skill on eval 3's key finding. A strong general-purpose agent with Bash/Grep is already quite capable at this kind of investigation.
with_skill was faster in all 3 evals (mean 256.7s vs 324.5s, -21%) - the scan.mjs script replaces a lot of ad-hoc `du`/version-reading tool calls with one deterministic pass.

Token usage did not consistently favor with_skill: it used fewer tokens in eval 1 and eval 3 but ~34% MORE in eval 2 than its own baseline - worth a closer look at what eval 2's with_skill run spent extra tool calls on.

Baseline (eval 1) is the one clear quality miss: it conflated ordinary patch-level version differences (expected with 5 independent lockfiles) with 'real drift found', which the skill's explicit majorDrift-only framing avoids - this is the skill's clearest, most reproducible value-add across the three evals, more than raw finding-power.

The skill's structural consistency (same 4-section template, same units, same mermaid diagram shape every time) is a real advantage for a report meant to be read repeatedly by a team, even though it didn't show up as a per-eval pass/fail difference here.
